guidance: Canonicalization fixes a representation; it does not sign, encrypt or validate anything. A matching hash shows the bytes did not change, not who wrote them. Numbers are IEEE-754 doubles, so an integer beyond ±2^53 is rounded, and the page warns when that happens.
method: JSON Canonicalization Scheme (RFC 8785). The document is parsed, then serialized with no whitespace: every object's property names are compared in their unescaped form as arrays of UTF-16 code units (unsigned integers, independent of locale) and sorted recursively, while array element order is preserved. Strings are serialized as ECMAScript's JSON.stringify does: U+0008, U+0009, U+000A, U+000C and U+000D use \b, \t, \n, \f and \r, every other character from U+0000 to U+001F uses lowercase \uhhhh, quote and backslash are escaped, and every code point outside the control range is written as is. Numbers are ECMAScript Number::toString of the IEEE-754 double, so 1E30 becomes 1e+30, 4.50 becomes 4.5, -0 becomes 0 and 1e-7 stays in exponent form until 1e-6. The result is encoded as UTF-8. Input that I-JSON excludes is refused with a sentence naming the line and column: duplicate property names, unpaired surrogates, NaN or Infinity, numbers outside the double range, unescaped control characters, and malformed JSON. Documents are capped at 200,000 characters and 128 levels of nesting, and a byte-order mark is skipped. An integer literal outside the ±2^53 range is accepted as the nearest double, with a warning that shows the value written into the output. The page reports the UTF-8 byte length and the SHA-256 digest of the canonical bytes, computed locally with the Web Crypto API when the browser offers it. The implementation is checked byte for byte against the six input/output pairs published with the RFC 8785 reference code (arrays, French sorting, structures, Unicode, values and weird) and against Table 1 of Appendix B for number serialization; it is not a signature, a validator or an encryption tool.
